display.title: Hashem's Greatest Gift (Gimmel Tammuz)
display.summary_short: Before Gimmel Tammuz, a parable of a lost king, a poor Jew's stale bread, and why even a small hachlatah in the darkness of golus is Hashem's greatest gift.
display.summary_long: With Gimmel Tammuz a week away, the storyteller encourages children to make a good resolution as a gift to the Rebbe, such as saying a brachah slowly and carefully, or keeping the five things before bedtime: Shema, negel vasser by the bed, kissing the mezuzah, and sleeping with a yarmulke and tzitzis. When the yetzer hara says such a resolution is too small, a parable answers it. A king out hunting is lost in a freezing forest at night and finds the hut of a poor Jew, Reb Chaim, who welcomes him with his last slice of stale bread, a glass of water and a bed of straw. The king later summons him, reveals who he was and rewards him with a sack of gold. A neighbor hears and brings the king the same stale bread, water and straw in a box, hoping for the same reward. The kind king explains that in his palace such things mean little; in the dark, cold forest they saved his life. So too, every small mitzvah done in the darkness of golus is precious to Hashem, and He will repay it with the greatest gift, Moshiach.
display.lesson: No good resolution is too small: in the darkness of golus, every mitzvah is Hashem's greatest gift, and He will repay us with Moshiach.
